title: The soul you gave me is pure
hook: Elohai Neshamah: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure

segments.voice: Yesterday, a later blessing for people who wake up tired. Your line was enough to begin. Whose load did you lighten? Today, the end of this week, and the blessing for the soul. Day five hundred forty-six.

What's the first thing your mind says to you in the morning? For some people it's a list of failures. You didn't finish that. You said the wrong thing. You're behind. For them, the inner critic is awake first. Now put next to that the line the Talmud says a person should say on waking, before the blessings for eyes and legs and clothes. It doesn't begin with what you did wrong. It doesn't begin with what you owe. It begins with one word about who you are: pure.
screen: `THE INNER CRITIC WAKES FIRST.` → `A DIFFERENT FIRST WORD.` → `PURE.`

segments.voice: The prayer is called Elohai neshamah, my God, the soul. In the Talmud, in Berakhot, it runs roughly like this: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure. You created it, you formed it, you breathed it into me. You guard it within me, and one day you will take it from me, and return it in the time to come. As long as the soul is in me, I give thanks. And it ends: blessed are you, who restores souls to bodies. Now the word. Neshamah means soul, and it's close kin to the Hebrew word for breath. In Genesis, the old Jewish translation says God "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Breath of life there is nishmat chayim. So when the prayer says you breathed it into me, it's pointing back to the first human, and to every breath since. Notice the order of the prayer. Before thanks, before requests, before any confession, it makes a statement: the soul is pure. Jewish teachers point to this line to say that a person starts each morning with a soul that is clean. Mistakes are real, and the tradition takes repair very seriously. But the soul itself isn't the mistake. And the prayer is honest about death too: it says plainly that the soul will one day be taken. That's why waking is treated as a return. In the prayer's telling, it was given back again this morning.
screen: `ELOHAI NESHAMAH: MY GOD, THE SOUL.` · `NESHAMAH: SOUL, AND BREATH.` · `PURE, BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.` · `WAKING IS A RETURN.` · then, large: `THE SOUL IS PURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe and say pure. Settle, and breathe. Feel the air come in through your nose, cool, and go out, warm. Each time you breathe in, think of the word neshamah, breath and soul together. Each time you breathe out, say the word pure, out loud or inside. If the critic starts its list, let it talk, and keep breathing under it. In, neshamah. Out, pure. Nothing to fix for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Neshamah. Soul, close kin to the word for breath: the soul the morning prayer calls pure.

Your line: the soul is pure. A week of the heart's work, the doorway, the dawn blessings, the rooster, opened eyes, strength for the weary, and a pure soul. Today, when the critic speaks, answer it with one word: pure. Day five hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Elohai neshamah is said each morning among the morning blessings, at home or in the synagogue; many people also say the short Modeh Ani on first waking and Elohai neshamah after washing their hands.

original.note: Hebrew: soul, close kin to neshimah, breath.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pious line about having a soul.
what it means: before any failure or task, the day begins by calling the soul pure, and waking a return.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 60b gives the text; it opens without baruch and closes with the blessing over restoring souls, and neshamah echoes nishmat chayim in Genesis 2:7.
